name: Palimpsest Reach

detectability.signature: Duplicated stellar returns: every star near the fold appears twice at slightly offset positions, like a printed page showing text through thin paper

proximity: Background stars double and drift out of register as the fold's depth changes
Ships report faint radio echoes of their own transmissions arriving seconds late
contact: Transiting the fold displaces vessels along its crease, typically 0.01 to 0.05 AU sideways
Brief sensory doubling: crew see two copies of their own bridge for several seconds
prolonged_exposure: Chronic mild disorientation among navigators who work the crease daily
Gradual accumulation of micro-displacements leaves long-term residents uncertain of their true position by thousands of kilometers

behavior.cycle: Fold depth oscillates on a 19-day cycle tied to the crease's orbit around the system barycenter

phenomena: Ships exiting at different locations than entered, displaced along the fold's crease
Duplicated starfield: paired stellar images drifting in and out of alignment
Radio echoes of transmissions arriving seconds after they are sent
hazards: Navigation error: displacement at emergence can place a ship inside planetary orbit lanes
Collision risk during crease transits when traffic from both sides converges on the same exit window
opportunities: Shortcut through normal space: the crease compresses a 9-week crossing into 11 days
Strategic chokepoint control; whoever holds the fold's mouth holds the system's back door
Smuggling route favored precisely because displacement is hard to predict
known_incidents: In 2387 the liner Meridian Rose emerged from a crease transit 40,000 kilometers off her track, crossing the outbound shipping lane and shearing the antenna mast off the freighter Cold Harbor; new spacing rules followed within the year
Blockade runners used the Reach eleven times during the Kestrel Dispute, and the blockading fleet never once intercepted a transit
description: Palimpsest Reach is visible from the outer system as a subtle doubling of the heavens: every star within twelve astronomical units of the crease shows a ghost image, slightly offset, like ink bleeding through cheap paper. The effect breathes. Over a nineteen-day cycle the fold deepens and relaxes as it orbits the system barycenter, and the paired images slide together and apart in slow, tidal rhythm.

Crossing the crease is routine and mildly unsettling. Ships emerge displaced along the fold by up to five hundred thousand kilometers, and crews briefly see their own bridge doubled before the copies resolve into one. Navigators who work the route learn to read the fold's phase tables, but the tables only narrow the uncertainty; the last few thousand kilometers of emergence point remain the fold's private joke.

Engineers date the structure to roughly fourteen centuries ago and identify it as artificial: the crease follows a mathematically clean elliptical trace consistent with a deliberate folding of local space by parties unknown. The 2387 Meridian Rose collision with Cold Harbor's mast remains the Reach's worst accident and produced the lane-spacing rules still in force. During the Kestrel Dispute, blockade runners proved what naval planners had feared: the fold is a back door no cordon can close.

Today the crease carries scheduled packet traffic, a navy listening post at the fold's mouth, and more unregistered hulls than any customs officer cares to count. The nineteen-day cycle is published, the exit windows are auctioned, and the whole arrangement works with the uneasy efficiency of a toll road built by no one. Scholars still ask who folded the system and why; the pilots who use it daily ask only one thing, which is whether the tables were updated this cycle.
